news_drafts.headline: Merton Cabinet papers show £69.1m schools high needs deficit and £137m of revenue reserves
news_drafts.lead:
Merton's schools funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities (known as high needs) has been in deficit since 2018/19 and had grown to £69.1m by 31 March 2026, according to budget papers for the Cabinet meeting on 19 October. The council says that is the second highest such deficit in London. It estimates a further £23.3m will build up in 2026/27.

The deficit sits on the dedicated schools grant (DSG), the government grant that funds schools. The government's High Needs Stability Grant covers 90% of the historic deficit. Ministers have indicated similar proportionate support may continue for deficits arising in 2026-27 and 2027-28, but confirmation is pending. From 2028-29, the papers say, spending on special needs will be covered by the government's overall departmental budget, so councils will no longer have to fund future costs from general funds once the statutory override (the temporary rule keeping such deficits off a council's main balance sheet) ends.

Merton held revenue reserves (money put aside) of about £137m at 31 March 2026, the sixth highest of London's 32 boroughs; the London average is £132m. Its capital reserves of £181m are third highest in Outer London. The papers say these figures put the council at low risk on the Chartered Institute of Public Finance and Accountancy's Financial Resilience Index. About £58.6m of the earmarked reserves is intended to offset the historic schools deficit, conditional on the government grant. The papers state that if that support is not provided, the deficit would have to be met from general reserves.

news_drafts.headline: Merton expects £63.2m government grant against schools deficit forecast at £92.4m without it
news_drafts.lead:
Merton Council expects to receive £63.196m from a new government High Needs Stability Grant, which would cover 90% of the schools-funding deficit it carried forward from 2025/26. The figures are in the financial monitoring report for the first three months of the year, put to the council's Overview and Scrutiny Committee on 14 October 2026.

The deficit is on the dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools). Merton has overspent on it every year since 2018/19, mainly on high needs (support for children with special educational needs and disabilities). The paper says the cumulative deficit at the end of 2026/27 is £92.401m "without the stability grant". That includes a forecast in-year overspend of £23.275m this year, which the report attributes to rising numbers and greater complexity among children with Education, Health and Care Plans. The grant is worth 90% of the £69.126m historic deficit brought forward.

The grant depends on a plan for reforming support for children with special needs. Merton submitted its plan on 19 June 2026. The council must cover the remaining 10% from its own resources. It must also manage continuing yearly deficits after the statutory override (a temporary government rule that lets councils keep such a deficit off their main balance sheet) ends in 2028.

news_drafts.headline: Merton faces £92m schools funding gap as government covers 90% of deficit but reform plan approval uncertain
news_drafts.lead: Merton Council's Cabinet heard on Monday that the cumulative deficit in the dedicated schools grant — the government funding for schools — has reached £92.401m, with the schools-funding crisis now substantially offset by a new government grant. The High Needs Stability Grant will cover up to 90% of eligible deficits, leaving Merton to fund approximately £9.2m of the £92.401m shortfall. The grant is contingent on the council's school improvement plan for children with special educational needs being approved by government; Merton submitted its plan on 19 June. Separately, the council's savings programme is falling behind: it has achieved 77% of its £13.177m target so far this year, a sharp decline from 95% last year, with particular shortfalls in children's services and environment budgets. The council is also facing emerging pressures in adult social care placements, children's residential care, and temporary accommodation.

findings.headline: Autumn Budget scheduled 28 October 2026 with Local Government Finance Settlement expected mid-December 2026, covering 2027/28 to 2029/30 with significant uncertainty beyond
findings.detail: The Autumn Budget is scheduled for 28 October 2026, 9 days after this Cabinet report. The Local Government Finance Settlement is expected mid-December 2026, covering 2027/28 to 2029/30, with final settlement expected mid-January 2027. The council's budget projections for 2029/30 and 2030/31 are based on flat cash assumptions for government funding beyond the multi-year settlement period, reflecting the absence of actual government funding projections for those years. Final budget will be set by Council on 24 February 2027, after settlement confirmation.
findings.matters: Government funding announcements directly determine the size of the budget gap in future years; council's budget gaps for 2029/30 (£1.048m) and 2030/31 (£3.680m) assume flat cash funding, which may prove optimistic or pessimistic; lenders need to understand the government funding dependency and the risk of gaps widening if settlement is adverse.
findings.figures: Autumn Budget 28 October 2026; provisional settlement mid-December 2026; final settlement mid-January 2027; multi-year settlement covers 2027/28 to 2029/30; budget decision 24 February 2027
findings.quote: Following the Autumn 2026 budget the expectation for local government is that the government will announce the Local Government Finance Settlement in mid-December. It is expected that the Settlement will be multi-year covering the period 2027/28 to 2029/30.

findings.headline: Pay inflation assumed at 3% for 2027/28 and 2% in later years, above Bank of England CPI forecast of 2.9% moderating to 1.8% by 2029
findings.detail: The MTFS assumes pay inflation of 3% in 2027/28 and 2% for 2028/29 through 2030/31, with price inflation held at 2% across the full period. The Bank of England's July 2026 Monetary Policy Report forecasts CPI of 2.9% in Q3 2026, declining to 2.6% in Q3 2027, 1.8% in Q3 2029, and 1.9% in Q3 2030. The council notes that the position will be kept under review as part of future budget updates. These assumptions underpin the base budget and represent a material element of budget risk.
findings.matters: Pay inflation is a material budget cost driver; the 3% assumption for 2027/28 exceeds current CPI forecast and therefore carries upside risk; if actual pay settlements exceed assumptions, the budget gap reopens; the 2% assumption for later years depends on CPI moderating as forecast.
findings.figures: Pay inflation 3% (2027/28), 2% (2028/29-2030/31); price inflation 2% (all years); Bank of England CPI forecast 2.9% (Q3 2026), 2.6% (Q3 2027), 1.8% (Q3 2029)

findings.headline: Council moving to four-year MTFS model from annual budget rounds, with named delivery owners and milestones to strengthen governance and delivery confidence
findings.detail: The council is transitioning from annual savings rounds to a four-year financial strategy (2027-31) that starts with the full multi-year financial challenge and profiles savings and investment over the period with defined owners and milestones. This approach is intended to promote longer-term transformation proposals, ensure savings are supported by transformation capacity and evidence, and provide earlier visibility for scrutiny. The strategy establishes clear principles including that budgets must be aligned to the council plan and evidence-based, and that the budget will be balanced without relying on general reserves.
findings.matters: Better governance and longer planning horizon should improve delivery confidence and reduce mid-year budget turbulence; four-year approach allows transformation programmes to be established and resourced early rather than relying on late-stage efficiency cuts.
findings.figures: Four-year MTFS period 2027/28 to 2030/31; £28m savings programme with named owners and milestones across period
findings.quote: The Council is moving to a four-year delivery model that starts with the full 2027-31 financial challenge, profiles savings and investment over the MTFS period, confirms accountable owners and milestones, and tracks delivery throughout the year.

findings.headline: School-age population projected to decline from 23% to 20% by 2032 while elderly population increases, creating emerging mismatch with current service demand patterns
findings.detail: Merton's overall population is projected to increase by 3.3% (7,164 people) between 2022 and 2032, from 215,121 to 222,285. However, the demographic profile will shift significantly. Children aged 0-18 are projected to fall from 23% to 20% of the population, with primary-age children falling from 9% to 7% and secondary-age children from 8% to 7%. Conversely, the population aged 60-69 will increase from 8.7% to 10.2%, and 70-79 from 5.7% to 6.5%. The median age will rise from 37 to 38 years.
findings.matters: Indicates future demand pressures will shift significantly from children's services toward adult social care; current overspends in children's services may be transitional as the population base shrinks; long-term sustainability of children's service investments may require reassessment.
findings.figures: 3.3% overall population increase (2022-32); 0-18 declining from 23% to 20%; primary age 9% to 7%; secondary age 8% to 7%; 60-69 increasing from 8.7% to 10.2%; 70-79 increasing from 5.7% to 6.5%
findings.quote: In 2032, 20% of people are projected to be aged 18 years and under, down from 23% in 2022.

findings.headline: Sustained service demand pressures in children's social care, adult social care and temporary accommodation, with forecast 2026/27 overspends despite budget growth
findings.detail: Demand pressures are concentrated in three areas: children's social care (£3.084m overspend), driven by sustained growth and increasing complexity in high-cost residential placements; adult social care (£0.629m overspend), driven by placement pressures across homecare and nursing care; and temporary accommodation (£1.149m overspend), despite £3m budget growth, reflecting sustained demand. The council is taking action through early intervention, reablement and enhanced approvals, but pressures remain significant. The council acknowledges these as persistent structural pressures consistent with patterns across most local authorities.
findings.matters: Indicates structural demand-driven cost growth not being managed to budgeted levels; budget growth (£3m for temporary accommodation) proving insufficient; pattern across multiple statutory services suggests systemic issue rather than one-off pressure.
findings.figures: £3.084m children's social care overspend; £0.629m adult social care overspend; £1.149m temporary accommodation overspend; £3m budget growth (temporary accommodation); 724 temporary accommodation placements
findings.quote: The total number of placements in temporary accommodation at the beginning of April 2026 was 724. The forecast overspend on homelessness reflects the ongoing pressure experienced in 2025/26, mitigated by budget growth of £3m

daily_post.headline: PFI reserve depletion with three school buildings due for handover in 2029/30, requiring substantial future funding
daily_post.lead: School building handovers from PFI typically require significant capital investment; this is a known future liability approximately 3.5 years away that could constrain the council's capital programme and may require external funding or borrowing.
